```{r}
summary_stats <- function(x) {
  x <- x[!is.na(x)]                      # drop missing values
  c(n      = length(x),
    mean   = mean(x),
    median = median(x),
    sd     = sd(x),
    var    = var(x),
    min    = min(x),
    max    = max(x),
    q1     = unname(quantile(x, 0.25)),
    q3     = unname(quantile(x, 0.75)))
}

# Show that it works on one variable
summary_stats(mtcars$mpg)

# Compare with built-in functions
summary(mtcars$mpg)
sd(mtcars$mpg)
```
```{r}
two_sample_t <- function(x, y) {
  x <- x[!is.na(x)]
  y <- y[!is.na(y)]

  n1 <- length(x);  n2 <- length(y)
  m1 <- mean(x);    m2 <- mean(y)
  v1 <- var(x);     v2 <- var(y)

  se <- sqrt(v1/n1 + v2/n2)
  t  <- (m1 - m2) / se
  df <- (v1/n1 + v2/n2)^2 /
        ((v1/n1)^2/(n1 - 1) + (v2/n2)^2/(n2 - 1))   # Welch–Satterthwaite
  p  <- 2 * pt(-abs(t), df)

  list(mean_x = m1, mean_y = m2,
       t_statistic = t, df = df, p_value = p)
}

# Apply: does mpg differ between automatic (am = 0) and manual (am = 1) cars?
auto   <- mtcars$mpg[mtcars$am == 0]
manual <- mtcars$mpg[mtcars$am == 1]

two_sample_t(auto, manual)

# Check against R's built-in test, the results should match
t.test(auto, manual)
```
